faq.a: Milrinone is preferred in right‑ventricular failure, severe β‑blockade, or when pulmonary hypertension is dominant, because it also vasodilates pulmonary vessels.
faq.q: When should I choose milrinone over dobutamine?

faq.a: Only after a quick fluid challenge and bedside assessment that preload is adequate; mis‑using an inotrope in pure hypovolemic shock can worsen tissue edema.
faq.q: Can I start an inotrope before confirming the shock type?

faq.a: β‑blockers reduce contractility and heart rate, which can further lower cardiac output in an already failing heart.
faq.q: Why avoid β‑blockers in cardiogenic shock?

exam: A 58‑year‑old man with acute MI is hypotensive after 1 L crystalloid. What is your next step — explain why you would start dobutamine before norepinephrine.
A patient with severe malaria develops cold extremities and low urine output despite fluids. How do you differentiate septic from cardiogenic shock and decide on an inotrope?
Explain how bedside echocardiography changes your choice between dobutamine and milrinone in a patient with RV dilation.
A child with rheumatic heart disease presents in shock; why is milrinone preferred and what monitoring is essential?
Describe the dangers of using high‑dose dopamine in cardiogenic shock and why current guidelines favour norepinephrine plus an inotrope.
You have no echocardiogram. List three clinical clues that justify starting an inotrope and three that would make you pause.
During inotrope therapy the patient develops new atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. What is your immediate management and why?
Outline a step‑wise plan to wean a patient off dobutamine once perfusion improves.
ai.title: Inotropes in Cardiogenic Shock
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Inotropes increase cardiac contractility to restore perfusion in shock states. Use them after fluid optimisation, guided by bedside haemodynamics, and stop agents that worsen hypotension. Recognise when vasopressors or other support are needed.

b: Cardiogenic shock: SBP <90 mmHg, CI <2.2 L/min/m², pulmonary congestion.
Septic shock with myocardial depression may also need inotropes.
sections.p: Inotropes are drugs that enhance myocardial contractility, raising stroke volume and cardiac output. They are indicated when a patient has hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) with evidence of low output despite adequate preload.

b: Stage C: Persistent hypotension, lactate >2 mmol/L, oliguria.
Stage D/E: Consider adding vasopressors, mechanical support.
sections.p: Shock severity is staged by the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) classification: A (at risk) to E (extremis). Inotropes are usually started at stage C (classic shock) when hypotension persists after fluids.

b: Acute myocardial infarction (most common in low‑resource settings).
Severe valvular disease (e.g., rheumatic mitral stenosis with pulmonary edema).
Right‑ventricular failure from pulmonary embolism or severe malaria.
Toxin‑induced cardiomyopathy (e.g., herbal remedies, quinine).
Infective myocarditis (HIV, TB, viral).
sections.p: Identify the underlying cause of low output before or while starting an inotrope.

b: Cold extremities → low peripheral perfusion.
Elevated JVP with clear lungs → isolated RV failure.
Pulmonary crackles → LV failure.
sections.p: Patients are cold, clammy, with low urine output, cool extremities, and altered mental status. A rapid, weak pulse and narrow pulse pressure are typical.
If echocardiography is unavailable, rely on clinical signs (cold extremities, low urine output) and simple bedside tools (jugular venous pressure, pulse pressure).

t.b: What is the cardiac function and filling status? → Low EF or RV dilation confirms low output; guides inotrope choice.

t.a: Central venous pressure (CVP) or bedside ultrasound IVC
t.b: Is preload adequate? → CVP 8‑12 mmHg or IVC collapsibility <50 % suggests adequate filling; avoid excess fluids.
Is tissue hypoperfusion present? → Lactate >2 mmol/L supports shock; falling lactate indicates response.
Is acute coronary syndrome the trigger? → ST changes or troponin rise direct further reperfusion therapy.
Are there metabolic contributors or organ dysfunction? → Correct severe acidosis, hyperkalemia before inotropes.

b: New tachyarrhythmia → stop or switch agent.
Worsening ischemia (chest pain, ST depression).
Excessive vasodilation → hypotension despite inotrope.
sections.p: Inotropes can precipitate arrhythmias, increase myocardial oxygen demand, and cause peripheral vasodilation.

b: Dobutamine: β1‑agonist, preferred when SBP ≥90 mmHg and cardiac output is low.
Milrinone: phosphodiesterase‑3 inhibitor, useful in RV failure or when β‑blockers are present; watch for hypotension.
If profound hypotension (SBP <80 mmHg) add norepinephrine to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg.
Avoid β‑blockers and vasodilators until shock resolves.
Continuous cardiac monitoring for arrhythmias.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then start an inotrope while monitoring haemodynamics.

b: Transition to oral heart‑failure therapy (ACE‑I/ARB, β‑blocker) once stable.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce future decompensation.
Educate on early presentation for chest pain, fever, or worsening dyspnoea.
sections.p: Re‑assess cardiac output every 1‑2 hours; wean inotropes as perfusion improves and underlying cause is controlled.

b: Vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine) raise MAP but do not improve contractility.
Diuretics reduce preload; they are adjuncts, not primary agents in shock.
sections.p: Inotropes are sometimes mixed up with vasopressors or diuretics.

b: Normal CVP in early hypovolemia if the patient is on mechanical ventilation.
Lactate may be falsely low in chronic liver disease; rely on clinical perfusion.
sections.p: Certain bedside signs may appear normal despite severe shock.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent hypotension despite inotrope and vasopressor escalation
Rapidly rising lactate (>4 mmol/L) or worsening mental status
